consensus_summary: The consensus identifies the Ancient of Days as a symbolic title for the eternal God (typically God the Father), portraying Him as the pre-existent, sovereign Judge.
book_summary: The book identifies the Ancient of Days as the venerable One (God) who sits at the head of a calendar cycle, representing the origin and advancement of days.
consensus_core_identification: God as the eternal, pre-existent Judge.
book_core_identification: God as the venerable One presiding over the calendar cycle.
boundary_disagreement: The book adds a specific structural and calendrical function ('head of the cycle') to the title, whereas the consensus interprets the phrase purely as a metaphor for eternal pre-existence, ancientness, and judicial authority.
material_contradiction: The book explicitly contrasts its view with the common teaching by insisting the title includes a 'calendar office,' which the consensus does not recognize.
rationale: Both sources agree that the referent is God. The book refines the interpretation by shifting the emphasis of 'days' from an abstract expression of eternal age to a literal, mechanical role at the head of a calendar cycle.
strongest_objection: Daniel 7 focuses heavily on a judicial throne-room scene (thrones set, books opened, judgment given) rather than a calendrical system, making the 'calendar office' interpretation seem disconnected from the immediate context of the vision.
